newsitem.title: USA: Dollar gains, mark slumps after French left wins.
newsitem.headline: Dollar gains, mark slumps after French left wins.

text.p: The dollar surged and the German mark tumbled Monday after a Socialist victory in French parliamentary elections over the weekend raised doubts about Europe's proposed single currency.

France's new Socialist prime minister, Lionel Jospin, is expected to renounce the austerity measures advocated by Conservative President Jacques Chirac's outgoing centre-right government and push for a loosening of the strict guidelines for entry into the single currency plan.

This could lead to an increase in the number of countries qualified to launch the single currency, known as the euro, and weaken the value of the unit which is to replace the mark as Europe's paramount currency.

The mark, which has the most to lose from the introduction of a weak euro, fell sharply against the dollar and other currencies, including the Japanese yen, the British pound, the Italian lira, the Spanish peseta and the Swiss franc.

"It looks like Europe will go ahead with monetary union, but it also looks like the euro will be much weaker than people had expected," said Robert Sabia, vice president on the foreign exchange desk at ING Barings Capital Markets.
The dollar jumped to 1.7305 marks, up sharply from 1.7055 late on Friday, after rising as high as 1.7320 in the early afternoon, the highest level in almost a month.
The dollar edged up to 116.59 yen from 116.25 late on Friday, and made headway elsewhere as traders sold other European currencies amid the uncertainty over monetary union.
The dollar rose to 1.4340 Swiss francs from 1.4145 on Friday. The British pound retreated to $1.6357 from $1.6410. The dollar edged lower to Canadian $1.3752 from C$1.3775.
In France, the combined left -- Socialists, Communists and Greens -- won a majority of 318 seats in the 577-member National Assembly in the election.
A Socialist party spokesman told Reuters on Monday the coalition would seek assurances that the drive for monetary union would not signify further austerity for France.

Last week, a dispute between the German government and its central bank over plans to revalue the country's gold reserves sparked doubts about economic and monetary union, prompting active selling of marks.
And traders said they expect the ongoing debate over monetary union to become more and more heated in coming months, prompting further "safe haven" buying of dollars.

"Given the mess that the euro debate is going to create in Europe ... the best place to look is out of town," said Hillel Waxman, chief foreign exchange dealer at Bank Leumi Trust Co. of New York. "The dollar will be the prime beneficiary of that."
